Paper Content:
Co-MTP: A Cooperative Trajectory Prediction Framework
with Multi-Temporal Fusion for Autonomous Driving
Xinyu Zhang1∗, Zewei Zhou1∗, Zhaoyi Wang1, Yangjie Ji1, Yanjun Huang1, Hong Chen1
Abstract— Vehicle-to-everything technologies (V2X) have become an ideal paradigm to extend the perception range and
see through the occlusion. Exiting efforts focus on singleframe cooperative perception, however, how to capture the
temporal cue between frames with V2X to facilitate the prediction task even the planning task is still underexplored. In
this paper, we introduce the Co-MTP, a general cooperative
trajectory prediction framework with multi-temporal fusion
for autonomous driving, which leverages the V2X system to
fully capture the interaction among agents in both history and
future domains to benefit the planning. In the history domain,
V2X can complement the incomplete history trajectory in
single-vehicle perception, and we design a heterogeneous graph
transformer to learn the fusion of the history feature from
multiple agents and capture the history interaction. Moreover,
the goal of prediction is to support future planning. Thus, in
the future domain, V2X can provide the prediction results
of surrounding objects, and we further extend the graph
transformer to capture the future interaction among the ego
planning and the other vehicles’ intentions and obtain the
final future scenario state under a certain planning action.
We evaluate the Co-MTP framework on the real-world dataset
V2X-Seq, and the results show that Co-MTP achieves state-ofthe-art performance and that both history and future fusion
can greatly benefit prediction. Our code is available on our
project website: https://xiaomiaozhang.github.io/Co-MTP/
I. INTRODUCTION
Autonomous vehicles (AVs) should interact with complex
and dynamic environments to ensure safe and efficient operation [1]–[3]. Thus, the trajectory prediction has attracted the
community’s attention [4]–[6]. The accurate prediction relies
on the comprehensive perception information, especially in
complex and dense scenarios [7]. The limited perception
range and occlusion always lead to catastrophic results [8]–
[10], however, most existing works assume that all surrounding objects are fully visible and have complete history
trajectories [11]–[13], which is unreal in real vehicle onboard
sensors. Thus, vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technology has
been an ideal paradigm for sharing information among agents
and seeing through occlusion. Nevertheless, existing V2X
efforts focus on the single-frame cooperative perception
[14]–[16]. Issues such as How to capture the temporal cue
between frames with V2X to facilitate the prediction task
and even the planning task, and how to fully employ the
V2X information in real-world environments with occlusion
are still underexplored and present deployment challenges.

In the real world, each agent’s sensor differs in capability,
accuracy, and coverage [17], [18], and the positioning of
these sensors can lead to varied levels of perception and
occlusion of the same object. The simplest method of trajectory fusion is association and stitching [19], but it cannot
handle the diverse errors from different sensors and still
faces the incomplete problem when multiple agents lose the
same timestamp in dense scenarios. Thus, it is necessary to
explore how cooperative prediction integrates and leverages
incomplete history trajectories from multiple agents to obtain
more comprehensive history information.
Furthermore, the goal of prediction is not merely to
predict the motion of surrounding objects but to support the
ego vehicle’s planning [1], [20]. Each planning candidate
represents a driving intent, and the vehicle should evaluate
each candidate by reasoning the future because the reaction
of the environment varies depending on the ego’s actions.
If the AV reasons the surroundings solely based on the
isolated prediction, it will become too afraid to drive and
will always consistently yield to other road users [21], [22].
On the contrary, proactive planning and prediction make AV
consider their intention first and the reason for the other
reaction. However, the ego planning trajectory is the only
future feature in the future domain, leading to aggressive
driving behaviors and danger. Thus, for planning-oriented
prediction, it is necessary not only to incorporate history
interactions but also to consider future interactions among
surrounding objects.
To address these challenges, we present Co-MTP, a
Cooperative Multi-Temporal fusion Prediction framework.
First, the infrastructure, with elevated and stationary perspectives, can provide perception and prediction support to each
agent in the scenario, e.g. AV, human driver, and pedestrian.
Second, when AV drives into the infrastructure area, it can
receive the infrastructure’s history and prediction information, and fuse them in both history and future domains with
the planning information of the ego vehicle to facilitate
the planning-oriented prediction. Our contributions can be
summarized as follows:
• We propose Co-MTP, a general cooperative trajectory
prediction framework with multi-temporal fusion across
both history and future domains. Co-MTP is the first
framework to fully fuse and exploit comprehensive
temporal information in prediction with V2X.
• For the issue of incomplete trajectory in the history
domain, we designed a heterogeneous graph to learn
the fusion of the history feature from multiple agents
with transformers.

• To facilitate the following planning, we further extended

other vehicles’ actions from infrastructure prediction.
• We evaluate the Co-MTP framework on real-world
dataset V2X-Seq. The results demonstrate its state-ofthe-art performance, and both history and future fusion
can greatly benefit prediction and planning.
II. RELATED WORK
Cooperative Prediction. The existing effort of V2X research focuses on cooperative perception, and cooperative
prediction which considers the temporal information with
V2X is still in its infancy [23]–[25]. V2VNet [26] is the
first work to explore this field, which proposed an end-toend perception and prediction model. However, its prediction
head is simple and ignores the map information and complex
interaction features. Yu, et al. [19] presented a open-source
V2X sequence dataset for cooperative prediction, V2X-Seq.
V2XPnP [25] provides an open-source general framework
and V2X sequential dataset for end-to-end cooperative perception and prediction. Furthermore, the V2X-Graph [18] is
proposed based on V2X-Seq, which provides a graph neural
network (GNN) to learn the cooperative trajectory representations. However, how to fully employ the V2X temporal
information, such as the different temporal domains, and fuse
the cooperative trajectory still needs to be explored.
Planning-informed Prediction. The couple of prediction
and planning is the focus for safe driving in interaction
scenarios [1], [27]. PiP model [22] directly incorporated
the planning information into prediction, and Liu, et al.
[21] and Huang, et al. [20], further merge the prediction
module and general optimization-based planning module
[28], [29] to construct a reaction framework. However, only
considering ego planning in the future domain will inadvertently overestimate its priority on the road, leading to overly
optimistic predictions and potentially hazardous behaviors
[30]. Therefore, it is crucial to integrate the future intentions
of other vehicles during prediction to ensure a comprehensive
extraction of interaction features across both history and
future domains. The other’s intention is prediction targets in
single-vehicle prediction, and the ego vehicle not only can
access history information to see through occlusion, but also
the future information as the prior knowledge.

III. METHODOLOGY
Fig. 1 illustrates the Co-MTP framework. Both AVs and
infrastructures can operate prediction individually to support
the AV and scenario object separately. The input of the
vehicle-side prediction model is not limited to the history
domain but also includes the prediction results from the
infrastructure-side prediction model in the future domain.

B. Scene Representing with Graph
Heterogeneous Graph. The driving scenario has a lot of
heterogeneous elements, such as map, trajectories, different
object types and traffic signals. To leverage the powerful
scenario-representation capabilities, we build a heterogeneous graph for prediction scenario G = {N ,E }, where
N
and E present the set of nodes and edges separately.
Objects and the map are represented as graph nodes, and the
relationships between them are represented as edges between
the nodes. To represent heterogeneity, we construct a type
mapping function T for the nodes and define the type of
each edge based on its originating node.
Trajectory Data Preprocess. In Co-MTP framework, objects’ history trajectories come from both the AV and infrastructure perspectives, along with the corresponding mask
matrices. Before learning and fusing the information from
these perspectives, we follow the stitch method CBMOT
[36] in V2X-Seq [19] to use the high-detection-score to
interpolate the vehicle history trajectory with infrastructure
history, and the masks also are reorganized. We found the
prestitch of the incomplete trajectory can complement the
temporal index and accelerate the learning of the following
trajectory fusion. This prestitch method does not mean that
the infrastructure information not involved in the interpolation is discarded. All the original objects’ history trajectories
from the infrastructure are encoded in the graph nodes. In the
future domain, in addition to the AV’s planning trajectory,
the infrastructure’s prediction results of the other objects
are also included. Since our research does not focus on the
infrastructure’s prediction task itself, we use the our Co-MTP
model with only infrastructure information to output other
agents’ predicted trajectories.
To reduce the computational burden, the number of edges
for each node has the upper boundary. Whether the node
nnn can establish an edge with the node sss depends on the
distance between them. For object nodes, we use the position
observed at the last time step th to calculate the distance to
others. For map nodes, the shortest distance from other nodes
to the polyline or polygon is selected.
C. Relative Spatial-Temporal Encoding
Local Coordinate System. To facilitate interaction learning
in a normalized form, each node requires a local coordinate
system (xref,yref,θref) to provide a unique motion representation for each object, regardless of its global coordinates. All
subsequent computations related to the node will be carried
out within this local coordinate system. The position and
heading of each object at the final time step th are taken as
(xref,yref) and θref. For map data, the center point coordinates
are used as (xref,yref), and the direction of the longest line
segment within the polyline or polygon is treated as θref.
Graph Node Encoding. All the positions of objects from
both AV and infrastructure are encoded with a sharedparameter MLP. Then, the position features are concatenated
with other information (e.g. bounding box and speed) input
into two distinct MLPs—one designed for the AV and the
other for the infrastructure with different parameters. We
employ two self-attention layers to capture the temporal
features of each object in both history and future domains.
Since the history trajectory may be incomplete, the mask
vector mmmi is also input to the temporal encoding. For map
data, we combine the MLP used for coordinate encoding with
an improved PointNet to form the map position encoding
method. Additionally, we use a set of Linear layers and
GRUs to encode traffic signals. Thus, all nodes have been
encoded into a high-dimensional embedding, which includes
position, heading, speed, and mask information for objects,
and the position, direction, and signal status for map nodes.

D. CTCA Fusion
The CTCA Fusion consists of K Transformer layers,
each with self-attention and cross-attention. The self-attention
is used to process the nodes’ hidden features in the local
coordinate system, while the cross-attention is used to process
the edges between nodes. The CTCA fusion processes the
nodes and edges selected by the STSA module over K layers.
Finally, the features of the nodes and edges selected by the
STSA module are updated through the K layers of self-attention
and cross-attention.

E. Multimodal Decoder
The multimodal decoder takes the nodes’ hidden features
from the last CTCA layer and injects them into the Multimodal
Decoder, which outputs the multimodal trajectory prediction
results. The Multimodal Decoder is implemented with a
MLP that includes a softmax layer, allowing for the output of
multiple probability distributions over the possible future
trajectories.

III. METHODOLOGY (Continued)
E. Multimodal Decoder
The multimodal decoder takes the nodes’ hidden features from the last CTCA layer and injects them into the Multimodal
Decoder, which outputs the multimodal trajectory prediction results. The Multimodal Decoder is implemented with a
MLP that includes a softmax layer, allowing for the output of
multiple probability distributions over the possible future
trajectories.

IV. EXPERIMENTATION
A. Dataset Selection
We evaluated our Co-MTP framework on the V2X-Seq dataset, which contains a variety of real-world driving scenarios with
multiple viewpoints. The dataset is divided into training,
validation, and test sets, with the test set used to evaluate
the performance of the framework. We also conducted ablation
studies to demonstrate the importance of each component in
the framework.

B. Model Configuration
We selected the number of Transformer layers K = 3 for
the CTCA Fusion module, and set the number of attention
heads per layer to 4. The embedding dimension was set to
512, and the hidden size of the Multimodal Decoder was
512 as well. The learning rate was set to 2e-4, and the
weight decay was 1e-4. We used the AdamW optimizer
with a learning rate decay schedule. The training process
began with 5000 iterations, and the model was evaluated
every 500 iterations. For the graph node encoder, we used
a two-layer MLP with 256 hidden units each. The point
set encoder was implemented with a PointNet++ [37], which
was modified to include the map information and signal status
for each node.

C. Performance Metrics
We used the Mean Intersection over Boxes (mIoB) score
as the primary evaluation metric for the prediction task. For
the planning-oriented prediction task, we used the mIoB score
as well, but with a different weighting scheme for the
future domain. Additionally, we evaluated the framework’s
ability to predict the future by using the mIoB score with
the quintic curve interpolation. The results were averaged
over multiple test cases to obtain the final score.

D. Experimental Comparisons
We compared our Co-MTP framework with several state-of-the-art methods, including V2VNet [26], Yu-ET al. [19], V2XPnP [25], and V2X-Graph [18]. The comparison was done on both the prediction and planning tasks, with the results shown in Figs. 2 and 3. Our Co-MTP framework achieved better performance than the baseline methods in terms of mIoB score, demonstrating the effectiveness of the multi-temporal fusion and the extension to the future domain for planning-oriented prediction.

E. Ablation Studies
We conducted ablation studies to evaluate the contribution of
each component in the Co-MTP framework. The ablation
studies were performed on the V2X-Seq dataset, with the
results shown in Table 1. The ablation scenarios included
turning off the history fusion, the future fusion, the CTCA
Fusion, and the Multimodal Decoder. The results indicated
that each component contributed significantly to the overall
performance of the framework.

V.  DISCUSSION
A.  Contributions of the Co-MTP Framework
The Co-MTP framework addresses several key challenges in
autonomous driving, including the integration of multi-temporal
fusion for both history and future domains, the handling
of incomplete trajectory information, and the extension of
planning-oriented prediction to the future domain. The framework
proposed a novel heterogeneous graph representation for
the driving scenario, which effectively captures the interaction
